text: Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit
author: Jeanette Winterson
auditor_notes: 8 lessons audited (Eduqas only, english-literature-eduqas unit). Primary sources: Wikipedia, LitCharts character/symbol pages, SparkNotes chapter summaries, GradeSaver character list, SuperSummary, Goodreads quotes, Britannica, multiple blog reviews cross-checked. The novel's eight chapters are named after Old Testament books in order: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth. Chapter-level factual errors are the dominant issue in this set — the lessons repeatedly assign the Melanie love story and exorcism to 'Leviticus' (chapter 3) when they in fact occur in Numbers (chapter 4, first meeting) and Joshua (chapter 6, discovery and exorcism). Factual errors in plot, character, and chronology flagged; critical interpretation not flagged.

issues.location: L3 main body, key-fact box, and revision tip: 'The chapter title "Leviticus" is deeply ironic... by naming the chapter where Jeanette falls in love after the very book used to condemn her love'; key-fact confirms 'Winterson presents Jeanette and Melanie's relationship as natural and joyful — not sinful. The chapter title "Leviticus" creates structural irony: the biblical book of sexual laws names the chapter where Jeanette discovers same-sex love.'
issues.claim: The chapter title 'Leviticus' names the chapter where Jeanette discovers same-sex love and falls in love with Melanie.
issues.correct_fact: Jeanette first sees Melanie — working at a fish stall in the market — in the Numbers chapter (chapter 4 of the novel), not Leviticus. Their friendship develops and becomes romantic love across Numbers and into the Joshua chapter. The Leviticus chapter (chapter 3) is structurally about laws: it covers the mother's household rules, the market evangelism scene (Jeanette standing on an orange box in the rain), and Jeanette's first theological disagreement with the pastor. No love relationship appears in Leviticus. The structural irony the lesson attributes to 'Leviticus' is misplaced — the correct ironic chapter pairing is Numbers (where the love emerges) framed against the biblical Numbers (concerned with counting and ordering the community), and Joshua (where the love is discovered and punished) against the biblical Joshua (the conquest of the Promised Land).
issues.source: Wikipedia (chapter structure); SparkNotes ch. 3 Leviticus summary; SparkNotes ch. 4 Numbers summary; multiple sources confirming 'Jeanette and her mother go downtown and see a girl named Melanie working at a fish stall' in the Numbers chapter. LitCharts Numbers / Joshua summaries.

issues.location: L3 main body, first paragraph: 'Jeanette meets Melanie at church — Melanie is a new convert whom Jeanette brings into the congregation.'
issues.claim: Jeanette meets Melanie at church, where Melanie is a new convert.
issues.correct_fact: Jeanette first encounters Melanie at a fish stall in the local market, where Melanie is boning/de-boning fish (described as 'working at a fish stall'). Jeanette then invites Melanie to church, where Melanie is converted. The meeting location is the market, not the church. Multiple independent sources (Wikipedia, GradeSaver, SparkNotes, Vaia, Britannica) consistently place the first meeting at the fish stall. Describing Melanie as a 'new convert' at the point of meeting is also slightly ahead of events: she becomes a convert after Jeanette invites her.
issues.source: Wikipedia: 'her affair with Melanie (a fish stall worker)'; GradeSaver character list: 'She meets Jeanette at a fish stand'; SparkNotes/Vaia: 'Jeanette and her mother go downtown and see a girl named Melanie working at a fish stall. They soon become friends, and Jeanette invites Melanie to her church, where Melanie agrees to be saved.'

issues.location: L5 collapsible section on Miss Jewsbury and main body: 'there are suggestions that she has experienced same-sex desire but hidden it... Miss Jewsbury's secrecy reveals the hypocrisy at the congregation's heart'; and L5 key-fact box: 'Miss Jewsbury (hypocrisy exposed).'
issues.claim: Miss Jewsbury is a closeted lesbian whose sexuality is only hinted at, and who approaches Jeanette 'with ambiguous sympathy' after the exorcism.
issues.correct_fact: Miss Jewsbury's lesbianism is not merely hinted — when Jeanette flees the church after being publicly shamed (following the exposure of the Melanie relationship), she takes refuge at Miss Jewsbury's house, and that same night they sleep together. Multiple authoritative sources confirm this explicitly: 'when Jeanette takes refuge at the house of Miss Jewsbury, who is herself a lesbian, they sleep together' (SparkNotes); 'Miss Jewsbury comforts Jeanette and slowly begins stroking her, and soon the two are making love' (LitCharts). Miss Jewsbury also drives Jeanette to say goodbye to Melanie the following day. This is a significant plot event — a second intimate relationship — not an ambiguous suggestion. The lesson's framing ('suggestions', 'ambiguous sympathy') substantially underrepresents what happens.
issues.source: SparkNotes character analysis for Miss Jewsbury; LitCharts Miss Jewsbury analysis; SuperSummary: 'Ms. Jewsbury reveals that she is also a lesbian, and they make love'; GradeSaver character list.

issues.location: L4 main body bathos example: 'Winterson describes the departure without sentimentality: "I left and walked across the town to the ice cream factory."' Also: 'She gets a job at a funeral parlour... surrounded by the dead while trying to start a new life.'
issues.claim: After leaving home Jeanette walks 'to the ice cream factory' and works at a funeral parlour.
issues.correct_fact: The specific quote 'I left and walked across the town to the ice cream factory' cannot be verified and appears to be fabricated or significantly misremembered — no search source returns it. What multiple independent sources confirm is that after leaving home Jeanette works two jobs: driving an ice cream van (or truck), and helping at a local funeral parlour/undertaker (laying out corpses, washing the hearse, organising funeral lunches). The novel references an ice cream VAN, not an 'ice cream factory' — Jeanette drives it through town, and at one point notices the crowd at Elsie's house while doing so. The lesson is correct that Jeanette works at a funeral parlour, but the supporting quote appears inaccurate and the job description should reference both the ice cream van and the funeral work.
issues.source: Multiple sources confirm ice cream van/truck + funeral parlour: SuperSummary ('driving an ice cream truck and working for an undertaker'); search result: 'Jeanette finds work at a funeral parlor and drives an ice cream truck'; Vaia: 'She works odd jobs for money, including being an ice cream truck driver and helping at the funeral parlour.' No source returns an 'ice cream factory.'

issues.location: L4 main body: 'When she meets Katy, a fellow member of the congregation, Jeanette falls in love again.' L5 flashcard: 'Katy, a fellow member of the Pentecostal congregation.'
issues.claim: Katy is a fellow member of Jeanette's congregation.
issues.correct_fact: Katy is a new convert from Blackpool, not a pre-existing congregation member. Jeanette meets Katy at a tent mission event in Blackpool (described as a large mission retreat where Jeanette preaches). Katy is specifically characterised as a recent convert whose confidence about her sexuality contrasts with Melanie's submission. Multiple sources describe her as 'a new convert from Blackpool' and 'a recent convert.' The lesson's description 'fellow member of the congregation' implies she was already part of the church community, which is incorrect — she is newly converted when they meet.
issues.source: SparkNotes Joshua chapter: 'after a successful first night at the tent mission, Jeanette meets Katy, a new convert'; LitCharts: 'Jeanette soon feels drawn to Katy, a new convert from Blackpool'; GradeSaver: 'Katy is a recent convert.'

issues.location: L6 main body: 'Joshua, about conquering the Promised Land, names the chapter where Jeanette is expelled.'
issues.claim: The Joshua chapter is where Jeanette is expelled from the church/home.
issues.correct_fact: Jeanette's expulsion from home is the central event of the Judges chapter (chapter 7), not Joshua (chapter 6). The Joshua chapter contains the discovery of Jeanette's relationship with Melanie by the congregation, the public confrontation, and the first exorcism — and introduces Katy at the tent mission in Blackpool. It is Judges where Jeanette and Katy are caught in bed together, where the church and mother decide Jeanette is 'unteachable', and where Jeanette is ordered to leave. After the expulsion (Judges), Jeanette takes jobs driving an ice cream van and working at the funeral parlour. The L6 lesson therefore misassigns expulsion to Joshua when it belongs to Judges.
issues.source: SparkNotes / LitCharts / multiple: Joshua chapter = Melanie discovery and first exorcism, Katy met. Judges chapter = Katy discovery, Jeanette expelled, leaves home. 'Jeanette's mother wants her to move out of the house... Jeanette finds work at a funeral parlor' (Judges summary).

issues.location: L3 main body: 'Jeanette is kept without food for days.' Flashcard: 'Prayer, physical confinement and fasting for days — abuse disguised as care.'
issues.correct_fact: Multiple sources consistently specify that Jeanette was locked in the parlour for thirty-six hours (approximately 1.5 days), not 'days' (plural). The instruction came from Pastor Finch: 'not to feed her until she repents' for the next thirty-six hours. Saying 'days' slightly overstates the duration — though some secondary sources do loosely say 'three days', the most cited figure from the novel text is 36 hours. 'Days' is an imprecision rather than a clear error, but the flashcard should be corrected to 'thirty-six hours' to avoid students writing 'days' in the exam.
issues.source: SparkNotes Joshua chapter summary: 'the mother locked Jeanette in the parlor, and over the thirty-six hours that followed...'; GradeSaver: 'the pastor told Jeanette's mother to lock her in the parlor for the next thirty-six hours and deny her any food.'

issues.location: L6 main body: 'Leviticus contains laws governing behaviour (Jeanette discovers love and breaks the rules).'
issues.claim: In the Leviticus chapter, Jeanette discovers love and breaks the rules.
issues.correct_fact: The Leviticus chapter is about the mother's household rules and early theological questioning — Jeanette stands on an orange box at the market handing out pamphlets, encounters Mrs. Arkwright, and disagrees with the pastor for the first time. Jeanette does not discover love or break sexual rules in Leviticus. Love develops in Numbers. The structural parallel the lesson is trying to make (Leviticus = biblical sexual laws → Jeanette's law-breaking love) is a plausible thematic reading, but it is factually incorrect to describe the Leviticus chapter as the place where Jeanette 'discovers love.' This is a secondary occurrence of the OANF-001 error appearing in the structure lesson.
issues.source: SparkNotes Leviticus chapter summary; multiple sources confirming Leviticus chapter concerns the mother's rules and Jeanette's first theological disagreement, not the romantic relationship.

issues.location: L2 flashcard: 'She believes God will provide and refuses to seek medical help.' L2 main body: 'When Jeanette goes deaf (a real medical condition), her mother ignores it for months because she believes God will provide.'
issues.claim: The mother ignores Jeanette's deafness 'for months' believing God will provide.
issues.correct_fact: This is broadly accurate. Sources confirm the deafness episode occurs in the Exodus chapter and that the mother (and congregation) interpret it as Jeanette being 'in a state of rapture' rather than having a medical problem. Miss Jewsbury is specifically noted as the person who eventually takes Jeanette to hospital. The 'months' duration is plausible but not independently verifiable from secondary sources — no source contradicts it. The claim that God will provide is accurate. This is flagged as low-severity only because 'months' is an unverified specific duration, not because the core claim is wrong.
issues.source: Wikipedia: 'Jeanette experiences a three-month hearing loss in childhood — initially misdiagnosed by her mother and congregation as religious rapture'; LitCharts Exodus summary. Miss Jewsbury's role in seeking medical help: GradeSaver.

clean_lessons.note: No factual errors found in plot, character, or chronology. L1 (context), L7 (language/imagery), and L8 (themes/exam technique) are factually sound. The 'I miss God' quote, Section 28 timeline, Whitbread Prize, Pentecostal denomination, Accrington setting, and the chapter-title list in L6 are all correctly stated.

most_critical: OANF-001: Lessons 3 and 6 consistently teach that 'Leviticus' is the chapter where Jeanette falls in love with Melanie, building an extended structural irony analysis on this basis. In fact Melanie first appears in the Numbers chapter (ch. 4) and their relationship is discovered/punished in Joshua (ch. 6). Leviticus (ch. 3) is about the mother's household rules and Jeanette's first theological disagreement. Any student who reproduces this chapter assignment in the exam will be factually wrong.

OANF-002: Lesson 3 says Jeanette meets Melanie at church. Multiple sources confirm she first sees Melanie working at a fish stall in the market, and then brings her to church. The meeting location is wrong.

OANF-003: Lesson 5 describes Miss Jewsbury's sexuality as merely 'suggested' and her interaction with Jeanette as 'ambiguous sympathy'. In the novel, Jeanette takes refuge at Miss Jewsbury's house after the first exorcism and they sleep together — a significant plot event that the lesson completely omits.
